narration: Every evening, in thirteen million kirana stores across India, the same old notebook comes out.
Barely one shop in ten keeps its accounts digitally. The other nine still trust paper.
And one in three customers buys on udhaar — take it today, pay later, on trust.
Smudged names. Forgotten dues. Awkward reminders. Money already earned — that may never come home.
A shopkeeper with a queue at the counter has no time to type. He needs a khata that listens. So I built Bol-Khata.

Ramesh ne paanch sau rupaye udhaar liye. Done. Written to Ramesh's khata, balance read back.
Every customer has a complete khata — every entry, every promise, kept or broken.
When money comes back, just say so. The balance updates instantly. No pen, no maths.
A new customer? Just say their name, and their khata opens on its own.
This is the heart of it. The shopkeeper speaks naturally, in Hinglish. Gnani Prisma understands, the khata updates itself, and Gnani Timbre answers back, out loud.
Before giving credit, he can simply ask. Chauhan ji has already broken two promises — so, not today.
Sharma ji has always paid on time. Go ahead — he's good for it.

Every customer earns a trust score from how they actually pay. And when dues pile up, the agent makes the collection call itself — polite, patient, and it comes back with a date. In this demo, the customer is simulated.
Under the hood: Gnani Prisma listens, Gnani Timbre speaks, a reasoning model on Groq thinks — and a rule engine guards every rupee.
Thirteen million shopkeepers. No typing. No English menus. No forgotten udhaar. Just their own voice. Bol-Khata — your dukaan, your voice, your digital khata.
